title_options: The Physics Of The Smallest Motor Inside You ⚡
facts: Numbers and sources in tools/blender/hero/make_wiw_atp.py docstring; biology as fact-checked in the ATP book (research/hero/book_atp_ext/facts_checked.md).
sources: Yasuda, Noji, Kinosita & Yoshida 1998, Cell 93:1117; Lane & Martin 2010, Nature 467:929; Perry et al. 2011, BioTechniques 50:98; Watt et al. 2010, PNAS 107:16823; Noji et al. 1997, Nature 386:299; Campanella et al. 2008, Cell Metab 8:13; Fedorenko, Lishko & Kirichok 2012, Cell 151:400; Brand & Nicholls 2011, Biochem J 435:297; Kaminsky, Arena & Myers 2015, Mayo Clin Proc 90:1515
description: Inside your cells, a rotary motor about ten billionths of a metre across turns about a hundred times a second, powered by a membrane charged like a battery. We work through its physics: voltage and field strength, torque, efficiency, thermal noise, power, generators, short circuits and feedback. In 3D, from published measurements.

share.myth: Machines inside living cells are sloppy compared with human-made engines.
share.truth: ATP synthase turns in 120-degree steps with a torque of about 40 pN nm, and its work per step nearly matches the energy in one ATP, close to 100% efficient (Yasuda et al. 1998, Cell).
share.line: The motor inside your cells is close to one hundred percent efficient. A car engine manages about a quarter to a third.

scenes.narration: Inside you right now are motors so small that tens of thousands, side by side, would fit across the full stop at the end of a sentence.
Each one spins about a hundred times a second. And it's a real rotary motor, with a rotor, a shaft and a stator, like the motor in a drill.
It runs on electricity. Not from a socket, but from protons, pushed across a membrane.
Its name is ATP synthase. And this is the physics of how it works.
Chapter one. How much power do you need?
Even resting, your body uses energy at roughly eighty to a hundred watts. About as much as an old, bright light bulb.
Almost all of that is paid out in one molecule, ATP, the energy currency of your cells.
You hold only about a hundred grams of it at once. Yet you use about forty kilograms a day.
So every molecule is rebuilt about four hundred times a day.
The machine that rebuilds it is the motor. But first, it needs a power supply.
Chapter two. A battery in a membrane.
The motors sit in the inner membrane of mitochondria, the power stations of the cell.
That membrane is folded again and again, to pack in as many motors as possible.
Food is broken down until its energy is carried by electrons.
Those electrons flow down a chain of proteins, a little like a current through a circuit.
Their energy drives pumps that push protons, which are positive charges, to one side of the membrane.
At the end of the chain, the electrons are handed to oxygen, and make water.
Pile up positive charge on one side, and you get a voltage. Across this membrane, it's about a hundred and fifty to a hundred and eighty millivolts.
That sounds tiny. But the membrane is only about five billionths of a metre thick. Divide the voltage by that distance, and the electric field is about thirty million volts per metre.
Scientists have compared that to the field in a lightning bolt, across every one of your mitochondria.
Chapter three. Energy stored uphill.
The protons are pushed back by two things at once: the voltage, and the crowding, because there are far more of them on one side.
Together, they're called the proton-motive force. Like water held behind a dam, it's stored energy, waiting to flow downhill.
And the main way back through the membrane is through the motor.
Chapter four. The rotor.
In the membrane sits a ring. In animals, it's made of eight identical pieces.
A proton drops onto one piece, rides the ring around, and is let out on the other side.
Eight protons, one full turn. About a hundred turns every second.
In 1997, scientists in Japan attached a glowing filament to the shaft, and filmed it turning.
The shaft is only about two billionths of a metre across. The smallest rotary motor anyone had ever seen.
Chapter five. Torque and efficiency.
The spinning shaft turns inside a head with three working parts.
Each turn squeezes every part through three shapes, and each squeeze presses together one ATP.
Three parts, three ATP a turn. That's one every hundred and twenty degrees.
In 1998, the same team filmed the shaft clicking round in steps of exactly that size: a hundred and twenty degrees, one ATP each.
From how hard the filament was dragged through the water, they worked out the motor's torque, its turning force: about forty piconewton-nanometres.
Multiply that torque by the angle of one step, and you get the work the motor does for every ATP.
And that work almost exactly matches the energy one ATP carries inside a cell. The motor inside your cells is close to one hundred percent efficient. A car engine manages about a quarter to a third.
How can anything work that well? Part of the answer: it's tiny. At this size, water molecules are constantly battering it from every side.
The energy of that random jostling, at body temperature, is about four piconewton-nanometres. One ATP carries about twenty times more. Enough to beat the noise.
Chapter six. The power of one motor.
Power is torque times how fast something turns. Put in forty piconewton-nanometres, and a hundred turns a second.
One motor makes about twenty-five billion-billionths of a watt.
To run a hundred-watt light bulb, you'd need about four billion billion of them, all spinning flat out.
That's roughly the job your mitochondria do for you, every moment, without a sound.
Chapter seven. Motor, or generator?
Run an electric motor backwards and it becomes a generator. ATP synthase works both ways too.
Feed it ATP, and it spins the other way, splitting ATP and pumping protons back uphill.
Without oxygen, the bacterium E. coli does exactly this, spending ATP to keep its membrane charged.
Your mitochondria carry a brake, a small protein called IF1.
If the voltage collapses, IF1 largely stops the motors running backwards and wasting ATP.
Chapter eight. A short circuit.
Brown fat cells are packed with mitochondria.
Their membranes hold a protein called UCP1, a gap in the dam. Protons rush straight back through it, without passing through the motor.
In electrical terms, it's a short circuit. Current flows, but no useful work gets done.
So the energy comes out as heat, just as a short-circuited wire gets hot.
Newborn babies rely on it to keep warm. Adults keep smaller amounts, switched on by cold.
Chapter nine. Speed control.
Start to sprint, and your muscles burn through ATP far faster.
Every ATP spent leaves behind ADP and phosphate.
Those are exactly what the motor needs. As they build up, it spins faster, and the chain pumps harder.
Nobody flips a switch. Spending energy is itself the signal to make more.
Engineers call that negative feedback. And it's why you breathe harder: the chain needs more oxygen.
At full effort, a fit young adult can use roughly ten times as much oxygen as at rest.

So that's the physics of the motor inside you. A membrane charged like a battery. A field like lightning. A rotor turned by protons, stepping a hundred and twenty degrees at a time, close to perfectly efficient.
All of it, smaller than a virus.
Run an electric motor backwards and it becomes a generator, and this one does the same. So if a motor this small can be this efficient, what would you build if you could copy it?
